title: What Role Can Career Centers Play in Registered Apprenticeships?
summary: A practical guide for career-services teams on the three institutional roles in Registered Apprenticeship: training provider, intermediary, and sponsor, including responsibilities, internal coordination, and where career services fits in each model.
body_markdown:
If your career center is becoming more involved in Registered Apprenticeship, one of the first questions is what role your team should actually play.


Your institution may participate as a related technical instruction provider, an intermediary coordinating employers and apprentices, or a Registered Apprenticeship sponsor responsible for operating the program.


Each model changes what career services may need to support, from employer engagement and student outreach to recruitment coordination, advising, and outcomes visibility.


It also changes which responsibilities should sit with academic, workforce, administrative, or compliance teams elsewhere in the institution.


This guide explains what the training provider, intermediary, and sponsor models mean for career services, and how your team can help determine the level of involvement your institution is equipped to support.


## How Should Career Services Assess the College’s Role in Registered Apprenticeship?


The[U.S. Department of Labor](https://www.apprenticeship.gov/apprenticeship-industries/education) identifies colleges and universities as potential **training providers, intermediaries, and Registered Apprenticeship sponsors** . The A[merican Association of Community Colleges](https://www.aacc.nche.edu/implementing-ev-apprenticeship-programs/sponsor-intermediary-or-related-instruction-provider-determining-the-colleges-role/) uses a similar three-role framework when helping institutions determine how deeply they want to participate.


For career-services teams, the difference is primarily one of **responsibility and institutional capacity** .


College role Primary responsibility Program administration Relationship with employers May fit when...


**Related Technical Instruction provider** Deliver instruction aligned with the apprenticeship occupation Limited to the education component Collaborates on curriculum and training needs The college has relevant faculty, curriculum, and instructional capacity but does not want to administer the RAP


**Intermediary** Connect and coordinate employers, apprentices, education, and program services Supports portions of program development or administration Works directly across one or multiple employers The institution wants a larger employer-facing role without assuming full sponsor responsibility


**RAP sponsor** Administer and operate the Registered Apprenticeship Program Full sponsor responsibility Coordinates participating employers and other partners The institution has the capacity and commitment to manage the program itself


The right model is not necessarily the one with the greatest institutional involvement.


An institution may create substantial value by doing one part well, such as delivering related instruction, while an employer or another organization retains responsibility for the[Registered Apprenticeship Program](https://www.hiration.com/blog/registered-apprenticeships-guide-higher-ed-career-centers/) .


The implications for career services become more significant as the institution moves from **instruction → coordination → program ownership** .


## What Does the Training Provider Model Mean for Career Services?


Serving as a Related Technical Instruction, or RTI, provider is the most education-centered of the three roles. Under this model, the institution provides the academic or technical instruction connected to the apprenticeship while another organization operates or sponsors the Registered Apprenticeship Program.


[The Department of Labor](https://www.apprenticeship.gov/employers/registered-apprenticeship-program/partner) describes education and training providers as delivering instruction based on industry standards.


Their responsibilities can include working with businesses on apprenticeship curriculum, providing progressive credentials based on demonstrated competency, and connecting apprentices with academic or other support services.


[AACC](https://www.aacc.nche.edu/programs/workforce-economic-development/expanding-community-college-apprenticeships/intro-virtual-apprenticeship-network/implementing-a-registered-apprenticeship-program/sponsor-intermediary-or-related-instruction-provider-what-role-should-the-college-take/) similarly describes the RTI provider role as one in which colleges develop curriculum with employers around the skills required for the occupation. Colleges may also connect the instruction to academic pathways, certificates, credentials, or degrees.


For career services, this model means understanding how the apprenticeship connects with the institution's academic offerings and where the career center enters the student journey.


The relevant questions become:


- Does the institution already teach the skills required by the occupation?
- Can existing courses be aligned with the apprenticeship curriculum?
- Will new courses or faculty capacity be required?
- Can apprentices earn academic credit, certificates, or progress toward a degree through the instruction?


Career services may not own those academic decisions, but the answers affect how advisors explain the opportunity to students, how employer-relations teams position the institution to partners, and which internal teams need to be involved.


This model allows the institution to contribute its strongest existing capability, education, without automatically taking responsibility for administration of the entire Registered Apprenticeship Program.


For career-services teams, it can also provide a practical starting point when the institution already has strong employer relationships or workforce-aligned academic programs but limited experience administering apprenticeship programs.


3 types of roles in registered apprenticeships


## What Does the Intermediary Model Mean for Career Services?


The intermediary role moves the institution beyond instruction and into coordination.


The[Department of Labor](https://www.apprenticeship.gov/employers/registered-apprenticeship-program/partner) describes apprenticeship intermediaries as organizations with the capacity, expertise, and networks to help businesses create, launch, and expand apprenticeship programs.


Community and technical colleges are among the organizations that can serve in this role.


For career services, this can mean becoming part of the connective layer between employers, education, potential apprentices, and the broader workforce system.


[AACC](https://www.aacc.nche.edu/implementing-ev-apprenticeship-programs/sponsor-intermediary-or-related-instruction-provider-determining-the-colleges-role/) identifies responsibilities that can include apprentice recruitment, screening and readiness assessment, employer coordination, curriculum development, and support with parts of program administration.


The important distinction is that an intermediary can take on meaningful operational responsibility **without necessarily becoming the Registered Apprenticeship sponsor** .


That makes the model particularly relevant to career-services and employer-relations teams when multiple employers want to participate but do not have the capacity to coordinate every component themselves.


An institution might, for example, provide a common point of contact across several employers, coordinate apprentice recruitment, align instruction with employer requirements, connect partners with workforce resources, and help maintain the relationships needed to keep the program operating.


Career services may contribute directly to several of those activities, particularly employer coordination, candidate outreach, recruitment support, and student communication.


The institution therefore needs more than instructional capacity. It needs staff who can work across organizational boundaries and maintain sustained employer and workforce-system coordination.


For career-services teams already functioning as regional employer connectors or workforce conveners, the intermediary model may build naturally on capabilities they already use.


## What Changes for Career Services When the College Becomes a Registered Apprenticeship Sponsor?


Sponsorship represents the highest level of institutional responsibility among the three models. A Registered Apprenticeship sponsor is the organization responsible for administering and operating the program.[The Department of Labor](https://www.apprenticeship.gov/help/what-apprenticeship-program-sponsor?) states that sponsors can include employers, associations, workforce intermediaries, community organizations, and community colleges.


For career services, this changes the context considerably.


The institution is no longer contributing one component to somebody else's program. It is taking responsibility for the Registered Apprenticeship Program itself.


[AACC](https://www.aacc.nche.edu/implementing-ev-apprenticeship-programs/sponsor-intermediary-or-related-instruction-provider-determining-the-colleges-role/) describes college sponsors as assuming responsibility for program design and operation, with the ability to manage employer participation, apprenticeship administration, recruitment support, curriculum coordination, and program data.


For career-services teams, that usually means closer coordination with whichever unit owns apprenticeship administration.


Sponsorship can give the institution greater control over how the program is structured and how multiple employer partners participate.


It can also allow a college to create a common apprenticeship framework that serves several employers, including smaller organizations that may not have the capacity to operate separate programs themselves.


That control comes with additional responsibility.


The[Department of Labor](https://www.apprenticeship.gov/help/what-are-costs-associated-sponsoring-registered-apprenticeship-program) states that administering and maintaining a Registered Apprenticeship Program is the sponsor's responsibility. The precise operating model and costs depend on how the sponsor structures areas such as instruction, employment, and partner participation.


Career services should therefore understand where its responsibilities begin and end before the institution moves into sponsorship.


The institution may need to coordinate responsibilities across workforce development, academic affairs, employer relations, student services, legal or compliance teams, finance, and executive leadership.


Career services may be central to employer engagement, apprentice recruitment, communication, and outcomes visibility while another team owns registration, administration, and compliance.

## How Can Career Services Help Determine Which Model Fits the Institution?


Career-services teams can contribute to the decision by helping the institution assess the responsibilities it is prepared to own rather than beginning with the label it wants.


[AACC](https://www.aacc.nche.edu/implementing-ev-apprenticeship-programs/sponsor-intermediary-or-related-instruction-provider-determining-the-colleges-role/) notes that the roles available to a college can also depend on state requirements and institutional capabilities.


A practical internal assessment can consider the following:


Decision area Question for the institution What it may indicate


**Instructional capacity** Can existing faculty and programs deliver the required related instruction? Strong basis for an RTI provider role


**Employer relationships** Does the institution already coordinate regularly with employers around workforce needs? Greater potential for an intermediary role


**Program administration** Does the institution have staff capacity to manage apprenticeship operations over time? Important before considering sponsorship


**Employer need** Are employers asking primarily for instruction, coordination support, or full program administration? Helps determine how much responsibility the college needs to assume


**Scale** Will the institution work with one employer or coordinate several employers under a broader model? May affect the value of intermediary or sponsor structures


**Data and control** How much direct visibility and decision-making authority does the institution need? Sponsorship provides greater program ownership


**Internal alignment** Are academic, workforce, employer-relations, administrative, and leadership teams prepared to participate? Becomes increasingly important as institutional responsibility grows


**Long-term capacity** Can the institution maintain the model after initial launch support or funding changes? Critical for more operationally intensive roles


Career services can add particular value in assessing employer demand, recruitment capacity, student interest, communication needs, and how apprenticeship would fit alongside existing career pathways.


This is not a maturity ladder in which every institution should eventually become a sponsor.


An institution with strong instructional programs may be most effective as an RTI provider. Another may have employer networks and workforce infrastructure that make the intermediary model more practical.


A college prepared to administer programs across multiple employers may decide that sponsorship gives it the level of control and scale it needs.


For career-services teams, the important question is which model gives the institution a sustainable role while keeping responsibilities clear across the teams involved.


## Where Does Career Services Fit in Each Model?


Career services can contribute to all three models, but its role should change with the institution's level of involvement. The following division is a **practical operating model rather than a federal requirement** . Exact ownership will depend on the institution's structure.


College model Career services can contribute through Likely partners inside the institution


**RTI provider** Student awareness, career advising, employer communication, connecting eligible students with opportunities, and supporting transitions between study and work Academic departments, continuing education, workforce programs


**Intermediary** Employer engagement, apprentice outreach, recruitment support, student communications, coordination between employers and students, and ongoing career support Workforce development, employer relations, academic teams, student services


**RAP sponsor** Employer engagement, apprentice recruitment, student-facing communication, career support, outcome tracking, and coordination with participating employers Dedicated apprenticeship/program staff, academic affairs, workforce development, HR, legal/compliance, finance


Career services is therefore unlikely to need to own the entire apprenticeship function.


Its comparative value is strongest where the model intersects with students and employers: communicating opportunities, helping employers reach relevant talent, supporting recruitment, preparing students for participation, and maintaining visibility into how apprenticeship connects with the wider career journey.


As institutional responsibility increases, however, career services needs clearer boundaries with whichever team owns apprenticeship administration.


For example, a career center can support apprentice recruitment without becoming responsible for program standards. It can manage employer relationships without owning academic curriculum. It can monitor student engagement and career outcomes without becoming the unit responsible for sponsor compliance.


Clear ownership becomes especially important under the intermediary and sponsor models because more teams are contributing to the same program.


## How Should Career Services Coordinate With Academic, Employer, and Workforce Partners?


Registered Apprenticeship crosses organizational boundaries by design. Employers provide workplace learning and jobs, educational partners can provide instruction, and workforce organizations can contribute resources, employer connections, or program support.


The[Department of Labor](https://www.apprenticeship.gov/employers/registered-apprenticeship-program/build/create) describes Registered Apprenticeship as relying on partnership networks and identifies educators, intermediaries, workforce development boards, and other organizations as potential participants.


For career-services teams, the practical requirement is to understand who owns which part of the model and where coordination is required.


Stakeholder Potential contribution


**Career services / employer relations** Employer communication, student outreach, recruitment support, career advising, outcomes visibility


**Academic departments / continuing education** Curriculum, faculty, related instruction, academic pathways and credentials


**Workforce or economic development team** Employer coordination, program development, intermediary or sponsor operations


**Student support teams** Academic, financial, accessibility, and other support available to apprentices


**HR / legal / compliance** Institutional agreements, employment responsibilities, policies, and sponsor-related obligations where applicable


**Finance / grants teams** Program budgeting, funding coordination, and sustainability planning


**Employer partners** Jobs, workplace learning, mentors, occupational requirements, and industry input


**Workforce-system partners** Employer connections, participant support, funding resources, and regional workforce alignment


**Registration agency** Program registration, standards review, and regulatory oversight


No single organizational structure will fit every institution.


A college serving only as an RTI provider may need relatively simple coordination between an employer, academic unit, and apprenticeship sponsor. An intermediary model requires stronger coordination across employers and program services.


Sponsorship requires the clearest institutional ownership because responsibility for operating the RAP sits with the sponsor.


Career-services leaders can help establish those connections without absorbing responsibilities that properly belong elsewhere in the institution.


The useful starting question for the career center is therefore:


**“Which parts of Registered Apprenticeship should career services own, which should we support, and which should remain with other institutional or external partners?”**


Answering that question gives the career-services team a clearer basis for contributing to the institution's choice between the training-provider, intermediary, and sponsor models.

## Wrapping Up


Career services does not need to own every part of a Registered Apprenticeship initiative, but it should have a clear view of where its responsibilities begin, where other teams need to step in, and how students and employers move through the model.
